metadata.note: The Barre and Chelsea Railroad and its predecessor of the same corporation, the Barre Railroad (incorporated April 9 1888, renamed September 18 1913 when it absorbed the East Barre and Chelsea). It had two lives. Until 1944 it was a granite-quarry road climbing from Barre to Millstone Hill, whose passenger history rests on Pathfinder Guide listings alone - drawn here only as the two short pieces that can be placed on surviving track, at the years those listings prove. From December 1944/1945 it owned and ran the former Montpelier & Wells River main line, a mixed-train passenger road with a public timetable, until it closed in November 1956; that feature shares its geometry with the M&WR's own feature in montpelier_wells_river_railroad.geojson, split at the 1945 change of operator (Rule 4). Never reached Chelsea.
sources: The Official Guide of the Railways, February 1952: Barre and Chelsea Railroad Company table dated September 30 1951 (Montpelier - Wells River - Woodsville with times; Barre - Montpelier block 'Freight Service only'); index of stations daggers Websterville freight only
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Open and anchored ends: barre-rr-barre-switchback ends 1893 [OPEN] (last confirmed, not a known end); barre-rr-switchback-bonds is a single-year 1889 [ANCHOR]. No source found describes a Barre Railroad passenger train, so the character of that service (regular, workmen's, excursion) and its end are unknown - Bill Gove's 'Sky Route to the Quarries' (2004) is the book that would settle it. Not drawn: Bond's - Lamson's (stops not locatable on a surviving grade); Bond's - Websterville, anchored to 1894 by the Pathfinder, because Fowler's chainage puts Websterville at mile 12 - nine miles beyond Bond's, apparently via East Barre - while the surviving track from the junction to Websterville is under half a mile, so the 1894 route cannot be identified; the East Barre branch and the Graniteville / upper quarry spurs (no passenger evidence). Main line: the exact day of the 1944/1945 change of operator, and whether the November 15 1956 last run itself carried passengers. Headways and speeds are all estimates.

properties.line: Barre and Chelsea: Montpelier – Wells River
properties.speed_source: estimate for mixed trains; not sourced from a timetable
properties.geometry_source: Copied programmatically, coordinate for coordinate, from montpelier-wells-river-main in montpelier_wells_river_railroad.geojson (OpenStreetMap abandoned roadbed tagged old_railway_operator=B&M, ODbL); not retraced
properties.geometry_quality: Identical to the Montpelier and Wells River feature for the same track. Drawn 37.0 mi against 37.9 mi documented Montpelier - Wells River (Official Guide Sept 1951 and Fowler agree; the ICC valuation gives 38.22 mi) - 2% short. The line was lifted in 1957 and survives in OSM only as disconnected roadbed fragments: the source layer's metadata states about 40 percent of the 37 miles is straight-line interpolation across unmapped gaps, which this feature inherits; those approximated legs are not individually named in the source and have not been re-derived here (the longest single vertex-to-vertex leg in the geometry is 2.3 km). Ends at Wells River; the ~0.5 mi the trains ran on over the Boston & Maine bridge into Woodsville, NH is not drawn. No later-alignment issue: the line was not relocated in the B&C era.

segments.note: The Barre and Chelsea Railroad bought the Montpelier & Wells River in December 1944 (Nashua City Station, citing Lindsell 2000 and the ICC; the Plainfield Historical Society says '1945 re-organized as the Barre & Chelsea') and ran the main line under its own name until it closed. 1945 is shared with the Montpelier and Wells River feature, which ends there. The Official Guide of February 1952 prints a 'Barre and Chelsea Railroad Company' table dated September 30 1951 with times at every station Montpelier - Fairmont - Plainfield - Marshfield - Lanesboro - Rickers - Groton - South Ryegate - Boltonville - Wells River (37.9 mi) - Woodsville; Fowler lists the stations of the 1953 B&C timetable; the Marshfield Historical Society holds an April 25 1954 B&C timetable card. These were mixed trains with a baggage-RPO-coach combine, No. 14, 'in service on mixed trains between Montpelier and Wells River right to the end of operations in November 1956' (Plainfield Historical Society, which also dates photographs of passengers in 1946, 1949 and April and June 1954, and a mixed with the combine 'several days before the end of service' in November 1956). The last run was November 15 1956 and the rails were lifted by March 15 1957. Whether the last run itself carried passengers is not stated; the year 1956 is supported. Headway is an estimate derived from 'the twice daily round trip run to and from Wells River' (Oct 1953) - two trains each way a day - not a timetable interval. The Barre - Montpelier piece was freight only by 1951 and is not part of this feature; see montpelier-barre-branch.
sources: Segment-level: the 1945 start is from Nashua City Station and the Plainfield Historical Society; service through 1951-1956 is from the September 1951 Official Guide table, Fowler's 1953 B&C timetable letter, the 1954 timetable card and the Plainfield Historical Society's dated photographs and last-run account. Headway and speed are estimates.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced on surviving track: Ayer Street (Barre) south along the active Washington County Railroad to the switchback where the line reverses and climbs east (the reversal point, not the tail track beyond it). Drawn 1.1 mi against ~1 mi documented (Fowler: Switchback at mile 1). No straight-line legs. Assumes the 1889 alignment and switchback are the ones that survive; that has not been verified against an 1889 map, so this may draw a later alignment than its era.

segments.note: The Barre Railroad, incorporated April 9 1888 and built 1888-89, climbed from Ayer Street in Barre to the granite quarries on Millstone Hill by a series of switchbacks - the 'Sky Route'. Its whole passenger record is two Pathfinder Guide listings read from John Fowler's Vermont station list: Barre (Ayer Street) in the 1889 Pathfinder and Switchback, 1 mile out, in the 1893 Pathfinder. No narrative source consulted describes a Barre Railroad passenger train at all, so whether these were regular trains, workmen's trains or excursions is not known. Passenger service confirmed to 1893 by the 1893 Pathfinder listing of Switchback. This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when passenger service actually stopped. Do not extend without evidence. (The Barre Daily Times of January 8 1912 reports two new passenger coaches bought for 'the Barre and the Montpelier & Wells River railroads' - suggestive of later passenger work, not proof.) Renamed the Barre and Chelsea Railroad on September 18 1913 - the same company, hence the same colour. The quarry line carried granite into the 1950s and part of it is still Washington County Railroad freight track; none of those freight years is drawn. Low confidence. Headway is a placeholder estimate, not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: Fowler, Vermont Railroads Passenger Stations & Stops, section 27 (z = 1889 Pathfinder Guide; Switchback '1893PG'). Construction dates from the ICC valuation. Headway and speed are NOT SOURCED.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced on surviving track: from the switchback up the active Washington County Railroad (old_railway_operator=B&M) to the junction near Lower Websterville, taken as Bond's. Drawn 1.4 mi; with Barre - Switchback that puts Bond's at mile 2.6 against Fowler's mile 3 (14% short) - the identification of Bond's with this junction is an inference. No straight-line legs. Bond's - Lamson's (~3 mi to Fowler's mile 6) is NOT drawn: the stops cannot be located. Assumes the 1889 alignment survives; not verified, so this may draw a later alignment than its era.

segments.note: [ANCHOR] 1889 is the single proven passenger year: Bond's (mile 3) and the quarry stops beyond it - Parkhurst's, Gazeley's, Shepard's, Langdon's, Lamson's (mile 6) - appear in the 1889 Pathfinder Guide per John Fowler's Vermont station list. Service certainly ran wider both ways, but no other year is confirmed by any source consulted. Do not widen this to look plausible. Only the climb from the switchback to Bond's is drawn: Bond's is placed at the junction near Lower Websterville where the Websterville and Graniteville tracks divide (an inference from Fowler's chainage and the track layout, not a located station), and Parkhurst's through Lamson's cannot be placed on any surviving grade, so the anchor's last 3 miles are omitted rather than guessed. Low confidence: no narrative source describes passenger trains on the quarry line. Headway is a placeholder estimate, not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: Fowler, Vermont Railroads Passenger Stations & Stops, section 27 (z = 1889 Pathfinder Guide). Bond's location is inferred, not sourced. Headway and speed are NOT SOURCED.
